item.text:
Based on the supplied text, the main issues are below. Some are clear exceptions or omissions; others are potential litigation arguments whose success would depend on agency implementation and judicial interpretation. This is a drafting review, not a conclusion that each provision is unenforceable.

### Coverage and definitions

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Training runs can be split.** The compute threshold applies to a “single training run,” which is undefined. Companies could divide work among pretraining, continued training, fine-tuning, or separate models and argue that no individual run crosses the threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Exactly-at-threshold models are excluded.** “Greater than” excludes a model trained using exactly \(10^{26}\) operations. A company could also stay just below the threshold, although the capability-based definition in section 2(1)(B) could still apply.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** The bill provides no measurement rules for counting integer and floating-point operations, including different numerical precisions, failed runs, or work performed across contractors. That creates disputes over whether a model crosses the threshold.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Nontraining compute is not expressly counted.** The threshold does not expressly include inference-time computation, search, tool use, or other capability-enhancing work outside training. A highly capable system could therefore avoid this branch of coverage unless the Secretary makes a capability determination.

5. **Sections 2(1)(A)–(B)—“Model” and “system” are not consistently defined.** The compute branch covers a model, while the capability branch covers a system; neither term has a definition or rules for treating ensembles, agents, or modified versions. Companies could dispute whether components, combinations, and derivatives inherit coverage.

6. **Section 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is vague.** “Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks” supplies no task universe, benchmark, human comparison group, or required margin of superiority. Different reasonable testing methods could produce different coverage decisions, creating enforcement and fair-notice problems.

7. **Section 2(1)(B)—Capability coverage depends on an affirmative determination.** Unlike the compute threshold, this branch applies to systems “that the Secretary determines” meet the standard. Companies could argue that an otherwise qualifying system remains outside this branch until that determination occurs.

8. **Section 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is undefined.** The bill does not identify which Secretary makes capability determinations. Commerce’s registry role suggests an intended answer, but section 6 separately names the Secretary of State, leaving avoidable uncertainty about authority.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure is specified.** There are no express testing powers, submission requirements, decision deadlines, notice procedures, or rules for revisiting determinations after systems change. General administrative-law requirements may apply, but they do not supply the missing operational framework.

10. **Section 2(2)—“U.S. person” leaves organizational and residency gaps.** The definition does not expressly cover permanent residents, LLCs, partnerships, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions matter principally outside the United States, where section 3 relies on this definition.

11. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not automatically covered abroad.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary does not become a “U.S. person” merely because a U.S. company owns it. A U.S. parent’s own development activities could remain prohibited, but foreign affiliates conducting genuinely separate operations present a coverage gap.

12. **Section 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** The registry threshold depends on a chip category with no technical specification. Operators could dispute whether particular accelerators, custom hardware, or multipurpose chips count.

13. **Section 2(3)—Facility size is a poor proxy for covered training.** A data center with exactly 50,000 qualifying chips is excluded, and substantial training could occur with fewer, more powerful chips or across several smaller facilities. No aggregation rule connects facilities participating in the same workload.

14. **Sections 2(3) and 4(a)—Facility boundaries and operators are unclear.** The text does not define whether a campus, building, leased suite, or cloud cluster is one facility, or identify the responsible operator in shared arrangements. Splitting facilities or responsibilities could complicate registration and accountability.

### Prohibition and exceptions

15. **Section 3(a)—The prohibited activities are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” have no specified boundaries. Companies could contest whether acquiring, importing, hosting, distributing model weights, or using an already deployed system constitutes a prohibited act.

16. **Sections 2(1)(A) and 3(a)—Coverage during training is uncertain.** A model becomes compute-covered only after crossing the threshold, but the bill also prohibits training such a model. The text does not explain whether earlier work on a run intended to exceed the threshold is prohibited, or when liability begins.

17. **Section 3(a)—Supply-chain participation is not expressly addressed.** The bill does not expressly prohibit financing, supplying chips, providing cloud capacity, or facilitating another party’s prohibited activity. Existing secondary-liability doctrines may reach some conduct, but mere support is not clearly an independent violation.

18. **Section 3(a)—Cross-border activity lacks location rules.** “Any person in the United States” does not explain how to locate remote training or deployment when personnel, servers, and users are in different countries. Foreign providers serving U.S. users could dispute whether their conduct occurs domestically.

19. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts more than ongoing training.** The exception removes qualifying existing systems from all of subsection (a), not merely from a requirement to stop training. Its wording therefore also permits continued development and deployment of exempt systems.

20. **Section 3(b)—A token early start could secure an exemption.** The bill provides no minimum work required for training to have “began” before enactment and no completion deadline. Companies could start nominal training before enactment and claim exemption for extensive work performed afterward.

21. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering of modified systems is unresolved.** There are no rules for deciding whether retraining, fine-tuning, expansion, or incorporation into a new system preserves an existing system’s identity. Companies could argue that substantial successors are merely continuations of exempt systems.

22. **Sections 3(b) and 8—The grandfathering cutoff precedes the effective date.** Training begun during the 180-day implementation period would not qualify for the exception, although the prohibition is not yet effective. The text does not expressly explain the transition for systems lawfully started during that interval.

23. **Section 3(c)—The safety exception has no substantive limits.** Any otherwise prohibited activity could be characterized as conducted “for the purpose of safety evaluation,” without limits on scale, duration, commercialization, or access. The exception could cover substantial training and development, not just testing.

24. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities and oversight are unaddressed.** The bill does not say whether safety evaluation must be the sole or primary purpose, or require approval, independent evaluators, records, or reporting. Commercial work with a safety-testing component could therefore generate difficult disputes over eligibility.

### Registry and enforcement

25. **Section 4(a)—Registration has no deadline or update rules.** Operators are told to register but not when, including when a facility first crosses the threshold. The text also does not require updates after ownership, operator, or capacity changes.

26. **Section 4(b)—Workload reports lack required detail.** “Describing the computing workloads” does not expressly require model identities, customers, operation counts, training dates, or claims to exemptions. Operators could submit broad summaries that offer little help in detecting section 3 violations.

27. **Sections 4 and 5—Registry violations lack a dedicated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other laws might apply to particular false statements, but the bill supplies no express penalty for simple noncompliance with the registry duties.

28. **Sections 2–5—Investigative and verification powers are missing.** The bill grants no express authority to inspect facilities, compel training records, audit compute figures, or require capability testing. Existing agency powers might help, but the text does not establish how officials obtain the evidence needed to enforce it.

29. **Section 5—Enforcement responsibility and procedure are unspecified.** The bill does not identify who assesses civil penalties, whether assessment is administrative or judicial, or the applicable hearing and collection procedures. It also provides no express authority for injunctions or shutdown orders; whether other law supplies those remedies would require separate analysis.

30. **Section 5(a)—The unit of a civil violation is unclear.** “For each day” does not specify whether multiple models, runs, or deployments generate separate penalties on the same day. That ambiguity affects both deterrence and the potential size of liability.

31. **Section 5(b)—Willfulness adds a significant proof burden.** Criminal prosecution requires a willful violation, while coverage and exceptions contain several uncertain terms. Disputes over what defendants must have known—and whether they reasonably believed an exception applied—could make criminal cases difficult.

32. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effect by 180 days. The better harmonized reading may be that no violation exists before effectiveness, but the competing dates invite disputes about retroactive civil liability.

### International coordination, duration, and legal challenges

33. **Section 6—Negotiation does not ensure an international prohibition.** The provision requires seeking to negotiate an agreement, not securing one, and the deadline’s wording is unclear about whether negotiations must begin or conclude within 18 months. Foreign actors outside section 3’s jurisdiction could continue operating regardless of diplomatic progress.

34. **Section 7(a)—The safety-review process has no initiating mechanism.** The bill does not direct or fund the National Academies to prepare a report, set a deadline, or specify what “developed safely” means. This could leave the early-termination mechanism practically unusable or contested.

35. **Sections 7(a)–(b)—The sunset overrides an apparently safety-dependent duration.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes a safety finding, but section 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. Companies could resume prohibited activities after expiration without any safety finding.

36. **Section 7(b)—No savings clause addresses expiration.** The bill does not expressly preserve pending proceedings, unpaid penalties, records duties, or other consequences when the Act ceases to have effect. General statutory savings rules may preserve some liabilities, but the treatment of ongoing enforcement should be explicit.

37. **Sections 2(1)(B), 3, and 5—Vagueness challenges are plausible.** An uncertain capability standard, undefined prohibited conduct, and broad exceptions are particularly consequential when violations can bring imprisonment. These features could support due-process challenges, though ambiguity alone does not establish that a court would invalidate the law.

38. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 3—The delegation invites challenge.** The Secretary effectively determines which capability-based systems fall under a broad prohibition, with limited methodological guidance. That could prompt statutory-authority or constitutional delegation arguments, although such challenges would not necessarily succeed.

39. **Section 3(a)—Some applications could raise First Amendment issues.** A sweeping ban on “develop[ing]” systems could reach research or expressive code-related activity, depending on its interpretation. Courts distinguish protected expression from regulable conduct, so this is an application-specific risk rather than proof that the prohibition is unconstitutional.

40. **Sections 1–8—No severability clause addresses partial invalidation.** The bill does not state whether remaining provisions should survive if a court invalidates one definition, exception, or application. Courts may still sever invalid provisions, but the omission adds uncertainty about the consequences of a successful challenge.
